newsitem.title: USA: Halifax container cargo up 6-8 pct in '96-official.
newsitem.headline: Halifax container cargo up 6-8 pct in '96-official.

text.p: Container traffic into Halifax, Nova Scotia, should post an increase of six to eight percent in 1996, as the port continues to reap the benefits of expanding business to the U.S. Midwest, port president David Bellefontaine said Thursday.

"(The growth) is coming from the Midwest," he said, noting that the completion of the Sarnia-Port Huron rail tunnel linking key industrial centers in Canada and the U.S. had shaved half a day off cargo transit time bound for the Chicago area.
"It makes sense that we can ship cargo faster into the U.S. Midwest than you can going through New York," he added.

Container business was likely to increase at a slightly slower rate of five percent annually through the year 2000, he said. The projected growth rates sharply trail the whopping 22 percent rise seen in 1995, he said, when a port workers' strike in Montreal forced shippers to divert cargo to Halifax.
Halifax's emergence as one of the leading ports on the the Atlantic seabord was a hot topic of conversation at the North Atlantic Ports Association's semi-annual meeting here this week.

While ports such as New York are forced to continually dredge sediment to keep the shipping channels open, Halifax boasts a naturally deep-water harbor that can accommodate newer and larger container vessels.
Lower labor costs have also been a boon for Halifax, shippers say, enabling the harbor to siphon off market share from the largest U.S. ports.

But Bellefontaine, wary of stirring the pot at this gathering of maritime officials, sought to play down the rivalry between ports. He pointed out that New York still receives more cargo bound for Canada than the other way around.

He did say that port officials were actively recruiting shipping lines to Halifax, following the addition in 1996 of new services from British shipping giant P&O and the Maersk /Sea-Land joint venture.
"We are negotiating with a number of carriers right now," he said, though he declined to name the companies involved.
-- Wendy Pollack, New York Commodities Desk +1 212 859 1640
